- *Blessed*: The Hebrew term *’ashrey* appears twenty-six times in the Psalms. While some translations use “blessed,” a different term (*barak*) is used for blessings ({{Psalm 5:12|Psalms 5:12}}; {{Psalm 45:2|45:2}}; {{Psalm 107:38|107:38}}). 

- The godly are people who trust the Lord and try to live in ways that please him. They avoid living under the influence of sinners. 

Those who do not fear the Lord are “the wicked” ({{Psalm 36:1|Psalm 36:1}}). They oppose those who love God, do right, and the poor and oppressed (see{{Psalm 10:2-13|10:2–13}}; {{Psalm 37:14|37:14}}). The wicked might seem devoted to God ({{Psalm 50:16|50:16}}). Sometimes they enjoy success, but it does not last long ({{Psalm 37:35|37:35}}). They will face sadness and ruin when they must deal with the results of their bad actions ({{Psalm 1:4-6|1:4–6}}; {{Psalm 9:16|9:16}}; {{Psalm 32:10|32:10}}). 

- People who turn away from God's path and rebel against him are sinners ({{Psalm 25:8|Psalms 25:8}}; {{Psalm 78:17|78:17}}). They commit serious crimes like adultery (being unfaithful to their spouse) and murder (compare {{Psalm 51:1-19|Psalm 51}}). 

- *sit in the seat of*: This expression describes a person who is controlled by sin (compare {{Psalm 1:2|Psalm 1:2}}; {{Psalm 26:3-7|26:3–7}}; {{Deuteronomy 6:7|Deuteronomy 6:7}}). 

- Mockers are people who disrespect and reject God's wisdom. Mockers hate the Lord and insult anyone who tries to correct them ({{Proverbs 9:7-8|Proverbs 9:7–8}}). They seek only the “wisdom” that justifies their actions. These bold people have little respect for God, his plans, or his followers (see {{Psalm 86:14|Psalms 86:14}}; {{Psalm 119:51|119:51}}, {{Psalm 119:69|69}}, {{Psalm 119:78|78}}, {{Psalm 119:85|85}}, {{Psalm 119:122|122}}). These three terms (*wicked, sinners, mockers*) describe all kinds of people who do not live in a way that pleases God.
The Lord brings true happiness to those who turn away from evil and find joy in him.

Psalm 1 is a poem about God’s blessings, promises and laws for people. It describes two ways of living. People choose which way they want to live.

One way of living is to obey God. This is the way to live well. It leads to enjoying the blessings that God has promised to give. For the Israelites (Israel), obeying God meant obeying the law of the Lord. This was the Mount Sinai covenant recorded in the Law of Moses. Being faithful to it led to the covenant blessings.

God’s laws helped the Israelites understand what God wanted his people (God’s people) to do. People who want to be blessed by God do what God wants done. This leads them to a life full of joy. These people are like healthy trees that bear good fruit. They are strong and steady no matter what happens. God provides for them like a stream provides water for a tree.

The other way of living is to refuse to obey God. It’s making a choice to do evil things. It’s a way that destroys people and leads to death. God brings judgement against those who choose this way. Many years later Jesus also talked about these two ways of living in Matthew 7:13–23.

Psalm 1 is a wisdom psalm. It sets the tone for the whole book of Psalms. The psalm clearly contrasts the happiness of godly people with the judgment of the wicked. In the end, the way of wisdom will triumph.

The psalm describes an ideal picture of a godly person, similar to {{Psalm 8:1-9|Psalm 8}}. This picture shows what the Lord expects from his people. It also points forward to the coming Messiah, God’s chosen king ({{Psalm 2:1-12|Psalm 2}}). 

The people of Israel did not live up to this ideal. The kings from David’s family also failed to meet it. Even the best kings could not bring about the lasting righteousness described in {{Psalm 1:1-6|Psalms 1}}, {{Psalm 2:1-12|2}}, {{Psalm 72:1-20|and 72}}. 

In the New Testament, the apostles use the Psalms to describe the life and work of Jesus the Messiah. Their teaching shows that Jesus alone fulfills the ideal of the godly person described in the Psalms. Only Jesus fully pleased God and secured redemption (rescue from sin), true happiness, and peace.

{{Psalm 1:1-6|Psalm 1}} also introduces a note of hope that continues through the Psalms. It looks forward to the final hallelujah in {{Psalm 150:1-6|Psalm 150}}). At that time, the Lord will remove all evil from his creation and bring blessing and life to his people.

The first two psalms serve as an introduction to the whole book of Psalms (called the Psalter). {{Psalm 1:1-6|Psalm 1}} presents the Lord's guidance in wisdom, while {{Psalm 2:1-12|Psalm 2}} shows God's rule over a rebellious and sinful world. Together, these psalms invite people to abandon foolishness, which leads to destruction. These psalms invite people to follow God's path instead, which leads to wisdom and salvation. The New Testament confirms that God will govern the nations through Jesus Christ, his chosen representative ({{Hebrews 1:5|Hebrews 1:5}}; {{Revelation 12:5|Revelation 12:5}}; {{Revelation 19:15|19:15}}).

{{Psalm 1:1-6|Psalms 1}} and {{Psalm 8:1-9|8}} form an *inclusio* (a literary pattern where the beginning and ending act like matching bookends). Together, they describe what God expects from the ideal person. These psalms compare the godly person with the wicked and praise the dignity and worth God gives to the godly (see {{Psalm 19:1-14|Psalms 19}}; {{Psalm 33:1-22|33}}; {{Psalm 104:1-35|104}}; {{Psalm 145:1-21|145}}). 

Jesus the Messiah, introduced in {{Psalm 2:1-12|Psalm 2,}}fully embodies this ideal. He is the Lord with complete power and authority, and the perfect example of true humanity. The New Testament applies Psalm 8 to Jesus, showing that God placed everything under his authority ({{Hebrews 2:6-8|Hebrews 2:6–8}}; see {{1 Corinthians 15:27|1 Corinthians 15:27}}).

- The law of the Lord is called *torah* in Hebrew. It means God’s instruction or teaching for his people (see study note on Deuteronomy 4:44). 

- Meditating involves inner reflection, which can be positive ({{Psalm 1:2|Psalms 1:2}}; {{Psalm 63:6|63:6}}; {{Psalm 77:12|77:12}}; {{Psalm 143:5|143:5}}) or negative (see {{Psalm 2:1|Psalms 2:1}}; {{Psalm 38:12|38:12}}). The Lord’s word is the object of godly meditation ({{Psalm 119:48|119:48}}). 

- *day and night*: This includes all times, whether walking, standing, sitting, or sleeping (see {{Deuteronomy 6:7|Deuteronomy 6:7}}).
Well-watered trees stay strong and produce plenty of fruit (compare {{Jeremiah 17:8|Jeremiah 17:8}}).
The future belongs to those who follow a righteous path.

The future judgment ({{Psalm 1:5|Psalm 1:5}}) will remove the wicked and everything they have done ({{Psalm 35:5|Psalms 35:5}}; {{Psalm 83:13|83:13}}; {{Isaiah 17:13|Isaiah 17:13}}; see study note on Jeremiah 13:24).
The wicked cannot endure the Lord's judgment. They are already condemned (see {{Psalm 5:5|Psalms 5:5}}; {{Psalm 7:6|7:6}}; {{Psalm 101:7|101:7}}).

- When God takes care of people who obey him and punishes people who do evil, it shows how God gives people what their actions deserve (see {{Galatians 6:7-10|Galatians 6:7–10}}). This is called "retribution." The wicked might appear successful for a short while, but their lives are short and meaningless in the end. God and the people who remain faithful to him will have the final victory (see {{Psalm 9:5|Psalms 9:5}}, {{Psalm 9:6|6}}, {{Psalm 9:18|18}}; {{Psalm 10:16|10:16}}; {{Psalm 37:20|37:20}}; {{Psalm 73:27|73:27}}; {{Psalm 92:9|92:9}}; compare {{Psalm 142:4|142:4}}; {{Isaiah 57:1|Isaiah 57:1}}). 

- People who live in a way that pleases God are happy ({{Psalm 1:1|Psalms 1:1}}; {{Psalm 5:12|5:12}}; {{Psalm 14:5|14:5}}). They are happy because God protects and cares for them, listens when they ask for justice, and secures their future (see {{Psalm 121:3-4|121:3–4}}). 

- A person's path is their life and character.

*plot*: The Hebrew verb translated as "meditates" in {{Psalm 1:2|Psalm 1:2}} suggests opposing the Lord through speech ({{Isaiah 59:13|Isaiah 59:13}}) or thought ({{Psalm 38:12|Psalm 38:12}}; {{Proverbs 24:2|Proverbs 24:2}}).
Their useless paths lead to death ({{Psalm 1:4|Psalm 1:4}}, {{Psalm 1:6|6}}), but sinful human beings join together to oppose the true God and his Messiah.

Psalm 2 is a poem for nations. It’s about God’s blessings and promises. It’s also about the king God set apart to rule over the nations.

Psalm 2 describes two ways that nations can choose to live. One way is to respect God and to serve him. This is the wise choice and is the way that nations live well. Choosing this way means that nations do what God wants done. Their leaders obey God and recognise that God is the ruler who has complete authority. They recognise that only God has the power to keep their nation safe. God wants all nations and all people groups to follow him. All nations who choose to follow him are blessed.

The other way of living is to refuse to obey God. This leads to nations being judged and destroyed. Choosing this way means that the nations don’t accept God’s authority or follow his commands. Instead, they do evil things. This makes God angry. These nations don’t obey the king that God appointed. God called himself the father of this king. In this way the king was considered to be the son of God. God gave this king authority over all nations.

The Israelites understood that the psalm was talking about God’s covenant with David. It was talking about kings from the family line of David. Psalm 72 described what kind of rulers these kings should be. They should judge fairly and do what was right. They should punish those who did evil. Kings from David’s family line ruled in Jerusalem.

Psalm 2 talks about God’s holy mountain of Zion. Zion was another name for Jerusalem. It was holy because the temple was there. But the armies of Babylon destroyed Jerusalem and the temple. After that, no more kings from David’s family line ruled.

So the Jews came to understand Psalm 2 as a promise for a future time. They were waiting for God to send a king who would rule as God’s son. They called this king the messiah. New Testament writers understood that Psalm 2 was a prophecy about Jesus. This was talked about in Matthew 3:17, Acts 4:23–26 and Acts 13:32–33.

This royal psalm describes the Lord choosing a king descended from David. It celebrates the mission of all the kings in David's family line. It also introduces the hope of an ideal ruler. This ruler will accomplish the Lord's goal of bringing all nations into submission ({{Psalm 2:11|Psalm 2:11}}) or to destruction ({{Psalm 2:9|2:9}}). The New Testament identifies Jesus as this descendant (see {{Acts 13:33|Acts 13:33}}; {{1 Corinthians 15:25-27|1 Corinthians 15:25–27}}; {{Hebrews 1:5|Hebrews 1:5}}; {{Hebrews 5:5|5:5}}; {{Revelation 19:15|Revelation 19:15}}).

The kings hate the Lord's established order in the world, so they want to be independent of him (see {{Psalm 36:4|Psalm 36:4}}). They plan to dominate the Lord's people ({{Psalm 31:13|Psalm 31:13}}; see {{Psalm 83:1-4|83:1–4}}). Their goal is to undermine the Lord's rule by overthrowing his Anointed One (or *his Messiah*). 

The Lord chose the kings of David's family line to establish his kingdom on earth. The New Testament confirms that Jesus, the appointed and anointed Son of God ({{Acts 4:26|Acts 4:26}}; {{Acts 13:33|13:33}}; {{Hebrews 1:5|Hebrews 1:5}}; {{Hebrews 5:5|5:5}}), fulfills the role in which these earlier kings failed.

*break Their chains*: These kings think that recognizing the true God and his chosen ruler will lead to their enslavement ({{Isaiah 28:22|Isaiah 28:22}}; {{Isaiah 52:2|52:2}}; compare {{Lamentations 3:7|Lamentations 3:7}}; {{Romans 1:1|Romans 1:1}}; {{1 Corinthians 7:22|1 Corinthians 7:22}}; {{Titus 1:1|Titus 1:1}}).

*enthroned in heaven*: The Lord's position in the universe is so secure that he laughs at humans who claim they can oppose his power and authority (see {{Psalm 37:13|Psalms 3 7:13}}; {{Psalm 59:8|59:8}}).
The Lord sees the human threat as unimportant. He offered a solution long before they rebelled. He will stop their unrest by appointing a human leader, a descendant of David, to rule the nations.
*My King*: The Lord himself appoints and establishes his anointed ruler. The word *anointed* means chosen and set apart by God for a special purpose.

*today I have become Your Father*: In the ancient Near East, people often believed in a father-son relationship between gods and kings. 

In Israel, the Lord adopted kings as his sons. God set David apart as his most excellent and exalted son ({{Psalm 89:27|Psalm 89:27}}). All descendants of David were the Lord’s representatives or agents. 

Jesus is an eternal member of the Godhead (the one God who exists as Father, Son, and Holy Spirit; {{John 1:1|John 1:1}}). He is also a descendant of David ({{Acts 13:33|Acts 13:33}}; {{Hebrews 1:5|Hebrews 1:5}}; {{Hebrews 5:5|5:5}}). Because he is both eternal and from David's family, Jesus uniquely fulfills God’s plan. He is fully divine and truly human. For this reason, he is rightly called the Son of God.
The Lord adopted the king from David's family to conquer rebellious nations by force (see {{Psalm 89:26-27|Psalm 89:26–27}}).

- In the Old Testament, the relationship between the Lord and Israel’s king can be compared to a suzerain-vassal relationship. A suzerain was a great king. A vassal was a smaller king who served him.

In this picture, the Lord is the great King. Israel’s king rules under his authority (see Deuteronomy Book Introduction, “Literary Form”). The Lord invites his anointed king to ask for what he needs (see {{Psalm 21:2|Psalm 21:2}}, {{Psalm 21:4|4}}). 

- All nations will be subject to David's descendant, the Messiah.

The Lord grants his chosen ruler the power to conquer nations as his inheritance ({{Isaiah 11:4|Isaiah 11:4}}; {{Revelation 2:27|Revelation 2:27}}; {{Revelation 12:5|12:5}}; {{Revelation 19:15|19:15}}), ending their rebellion, resistance, and independence.
The Lord is pleased when people submit to him and seek his protection. Wise people accept the Lord's correction and want to change.

- *rejoice*: Leaders should accept the Son as their true and only King. 

- *Kiss the Son*: Kissing was an expression of submission ({{Hosea 13:2|Hosea 13:2}}). 

- The Lord gives joy to those who fear him. *To fear the Lord *means to honor him, respect him, and obey him ({{Psalm 1:1-2|Psalm 1:1–2}}). The Psalms also say that the Lord protects those who trust him ({{Psalm 18:30|18:30}}; {{Psalm 34:22|34:22}}; {{Psalm 119:1-3|119:1–3}}).

This difficult time in David’s life (see {{2 Samuel 15:1-18:33|2 Samuel 15–18}}) helps readers understand the promises of {{Psalm 2:1-12|Psalm 2}} better. The Lord gave victory to his chosen king ({{Psalm 2:1-12|Psalm 2}}), but God controlled how and when this victory happened.

- A *psalmist* is the writer or speaker of a psalm. The psalmist here faces many enemies. Those enemies speak boldly and without respect ({{Psalm 4:6|Psalm 4:6}}; {{Psalm 12:4|12:4}}; {{Psalm 40:15|40:15}}). They question whether the Lord can really save him ({{Psalm 10:11|10:11}}; {{Psalm 22:7-8|22:7–8}}; {{Psalm 71:10|71:10}}). Their words trouble the psalmist because it seems the Lord will not answer his prayer. 

- These enemies hold great power (compare {{Psalm 2:1-3|Psalm 2:1–3}}). Unlike {{Psalm 2:1-12|Psalm 2}}, this psalm does not resolve the crisis.

This psalm expresses sorrow that the hopes from {{Psalm 1:1-2:12|Psalms 1–2}} have not been fulfilled. Even when surrounded by enemies, godly people should not doubt the Lord's just actions. Instead, they can trust in God's goodness and expect God to rescue them.

This group of psalms moves from an orderly world to a troubled one. {{Psalm 1:1-2:12|Psalms 1–2}} describe stability. The righteous person is blessed, and the Lord’s anointed king rules with authority.

In the psalms that follow, the tone changes. The Lord’s anointed cries out for help. He faces enemies, strong opposition, and evil plans.

It even seems at times that the Lord is far away. The psalmist feels confusion and distress instead of confidence and calm.
The psalmist compares his enemies' arguments ({{Psalm 3:2|Psalm 3:2}}) with the Lord’s help. The Lord acts as a shield for his people, turning their defeat and shame into victory and glory.
The psalmist looks away from his enemies and focuses on the Lord.

By focusing on the Lord ({{Psalm 3:3-4|Psalm 3:3–4}}) during his crisis, the psalmist can rest, confident in his safety (see study note on Psalm 4:8). The Lord cares for his servant. God protects him and keeps his mind and heart free from fear ({{Psalm 37:17|Psalms 37:17}}; {{Psalm 54:4|54:4}}; {{Psalm 119:116|119:116}}; {{Psalm 145:14|145:14}}).

The psalmist feels peaceful and confident because the Lord protects and cares for him. This shields him from evil and gives him a new understanding of reality ({{Psalm 23:4|Psalm 23:4}}; {{Psalm 27:1|27:1}}, {{Psalm 27:3|3}}; {{Psalm 46:1|46:1}}; {{Psalm 56:4|56:4}}, {{Psalm 56:11|11}}; {{Psalm 91:5-6|91:5–6}}; {{Psalm 118:6|118:6}}).

- The psalmist does not seek revenge. Instead, he waits for the Lord to take vengeance. 

- *Arise*: The psalmist asks the Lord to act now.
Waiting for the Lord's answer helps you grow in patience and strengthen your faith ({{Psalm 38:15|Psalm 38:15}}).

This personal lament includes: 

- a prayer for rescue ({{Psalm 4:1|Psalm 4:1}})

- a rebuke of the enemy ({{Psalm 4:2-3|Psalm 4:2–3}})

- advice to the faithful ({{Psalm 4:4-5|Psalm 4:4–5}})

- a statement of confidence ({{Psalm 4:6-8|Psalm 4:6–8}})

- The opponents of those who follow God rely on false beliefs, deceit, and idol worship. 

- *my honor* (or *my glory*): The psalmist's honor, or possibly the Lord's, is being challenged.

- Feeling angry is not a sin, but letting anger control you can lead to sin (see {{Psalm 37:7-8|Psalm 37:7–8}}; compare {{Ephesians 4:26-27|Ephesians 4:26–27}}, {{Ephesians 4:31-32|31–32}}). 

- Instead of acting on their emotions, godly people think about their circumstances overnight. They might be disturbed as they sleep, but silence opens their hearts to trust in the Lord ({{Psalm 4:5|Psalm 4:5}}).
*Offer the sacrifices of the righteous*: Redirecting emotions toward the Lord prevents a godly person from doing too much self-reflection ({{Psalm 40:6-8|Psalms 40:6–8}}; {{Psalm 51:17|51:17}}).

*the light of Your face*: When the psalmist speaks about God’s face, he is asking for God’s favor and peace ({{Numbers 6:25-26|Numbers 6:25–26}}). God’s favor can change a situation from darkness to light (see {{Psalm 27:1|Psalm 27:1}}). 

Confident faith protects against anger, resentment, jealousy, and a desire for wealth as the highest good. When God’s favor is enough, other desires lose their power.
Peace comes from God's blessing and protection (see {{Psalm 4:6|Psalm 4:6}} and {{Psalm 37:11|37:11}}).

The phrase *give ear to my words* appears in several prayers as a call for God's attention during difficult times ({{Psalm 39:12|Psalms 39:12}}; {{Psalm 84:8|84:8}}; {{Psalm 143:1|143:1}}; compare {{Psalm 17:1|Psalms 17:1}}; {{Psalm 54:2|54:2}}; {{Psalm 130:2|130:2}}). The needy ask their God, “Are you listening?”

This morning prayer ({{Psalm 5:3|Psalm 5:3}}) shows strong trust in the Lord's help and protection. The psalmist asks for God's response and waits for it ({{Psalm 5:1-3|Psalm 5:1–3}}). 

He describes the plans of the wicked in detail but stays focused on God. The psalmist knows the wicked cannot be with God ({{Psalm 5:4-6|Psalm 5:4–6}}, {{Psalm 5:9|9}}; see {{Psalm 1:5|1:5}}). 

He keeps returning to the Lord ({{Psalm 5:7-8|Psalm 5:7–8}}, {{Psalm 5:10|10}}; see {{Psalm 5:1-3|5:1–3}}), and then he prays for the godly community ({{Psalm 5:10-12|5:10–12}}; see {{Psalm 3:8|3:8}}).

- The psalmist starts and ends each day with prayer, looking for new signs of God's faithfulness and goodness ({{Psalm 143:8|Psalm 143:8}}). 

- *wait in expectation*: The psalmist does not demand God's grace but hopes for it (see {{Micah 7:7|Micah 7:7}}; {{Habakkuk 2:1|Habakkuk 2:1}}).

- *The boastful*: Mockers (see study note on Psalm 1:1), the wicked ({{Psalm 73:3|Psalm 73:3}}; {{Psalm 75:4|75:4}}), and the arrogant ({{Psalm 10:2|10:2}}) use their words to distort the truth and challenge the faith of the godly. 

- The Lord allows only the godly into his presence (see {{Psalm 1:5|Psalm 1:5}}). His holiness and justice do not tolerate oppression or evil actions. 

- *You hate*: The Lord rejects proud sinners (see also {{Psalm 11:5|Psalm 11:5}}).

- God promises his loving devotion (his covenant goodness and faithfulness) to his people (see {{Psalm 25:6|Psalm 25:6}}; {{Psalm 69:16|69:16}}; {{Lamentations 3:32|Lamentations 3:32}}). 

- *Your house*: The righteous desire to enter God's presence with awe and wonder (see {{Hebrews 12:28|Hebrews 12:28}}).

- God guides those who are obedient, submissive, and patient as they wait for him to lead, provide, and protect them ({{Psalm 27:11|Psalm 27:11}}; {{Psalm 43:3|43:3}}; {{Psalm 143:10|143:10}}). He does not guide those who expect God simply to approve their own decisions. 

- Following the right path of wisdom leads to the Lord ({{Psalm 27:11|Psalms 47:11}}; {{Psalm 61:2|61:2}}; {{Psalm 139:24|139:24}}).
The psalmist again describes the terrible acts of the wicked, who cannot stand in God’s presence.

- The psalmist prays for the justice and retribution that God promised against the wicked ({{Psalm 1:6|Psalm 1:6}}). The wicked are those who have rebelled against the Lord.

- The wicked set traps to harm ({{Psalm 38:12|Psalm 38:12}}) or trick others ({{Psalm 140:4-5|140:4–5}}).

- A blessing rests on all who take refuge in God (see {{Psalm 18:30|Psalm 18:30}}). 

- Joy and praise go well together. The godly rejoice when they see evidence of God’s rescue. They sing joyful praises as a new song (see {{Psalm 33:3|Psalm 33:3}}). 

When the Lord brings peace to the world, defeats evil, and rewards good people, they will have lasting joy ({{Psalm 9:2-4|Psalms 9:2–4}}; {{Psalm 53:6|53:6}}; {{Psalm 90:14-15|90:14–15}}; {{Psalm 118:24|118:24}}). 

- The children of God, who find refuge in him, love his name. To love his name is to love his very character.

- The psalmist cares not only for himself but for all the godly people. 

- A shield, here an image of God’s protection, deflects spears and arrows from the one holding it.
*do not rebuke me … or discipline me*: The psalmist does not clearly connect God's discipline with sin here (compare {{Psalm 39:8-11|Psalm 39:8–11}}), but it might be implied.
The psalmist asks for God’s favor and restoration at a difficult time.
The occasion for this lament might have been sickness or a mental or spiritual depression from which the psalmist sought healing.

The psalmist became physically weak while waiting for God's answer to his prayer ({{Psalm 6:6|Psalm 6:6}}; see {{Psalm 77:3|77:3}}; {{Psalm 119:81|119:81}}; {{Psalm 142:1-3|142:1–3}}; see also {{Psalm 101:1-8|Psalm 101}}). Fasting (abstaining from eating food) might have contributed to his suffering, but it is not mentioned.
The experience was so painful that the psalmist might as well have been dead, or perhaps he feared for his life.
*from Sheol?*: In the Old Testament, Sheol is the place of the dead. It is not necessarily associated with punishment.

- The psalmist feels deeply exhausted due to his spiritual distance from the Lord ({{Psalm 22:1|Psalms 22:1}}; {{Psalm 31:9-10|31:9–10}}; {{Psalm 102:5|102:5}}). 

- When eyes *grow dim,* it means the body is failing (see {{Psalm 13:3|Psalms 13:3}}; {{Psalm 31:9|31:9}}; {{Psalm 38:10|38:10}}; {{Matthew 6:22|Matthew 6:22}}).
In a closing note of triumph, the psalmist reasserts his confidence in the Lord.

*Pursuers*, a common term for *enemies*, actively look for people in order to harm or destroy them ({{Psalm 31:15|Psalm 31:15}}; {{Psalm 56:1-2|56:1–2}}; {{Psalm 71:11|71:11}}; {{Psalm 143:3|143:3}}).

This psalm includes the following: 

- A lament ({{Psalm 7:1-2|Psalm 7:1–2}}): The psalmist cries out to God for help and protection from enemies.

- An oath of innocence ({{Psalm 7:3-5|Psalm 7:3–5}}): The psalmist declares that he has done no wrong and maintains his integrity.

- A call for God's justice ({{Psalm 7:6-9|Psalm 7:6–9}}): He asks God to act against evildoers and defend the righteous.

- An affirmation of God’s just kingship ({{Psalm 7:10-16|Psalm 7:10–16}}): The psalmist praises God as a fair judge who rules the world rightly.

- A concluding hymn of praise ({{Psalm 7:17|Psalm 7:17}}): The psalmist ends with a song of thanksgiving, honoring God’s righteousness and deliverance.
An unknown person from the tribe of Benjamin remained hostile to David.

Like a lion, a wicked enemy relentlessly and violently pursues its prey ({{Psalm 10:9|Psalms 10:9}}; {{Psalm 17:12|17:12}}; {{Psalm 22:13|22:13}}, {{Psalm 22:21|21}}; {{Psalm 35:17|35:17}}; {{Psalm 57:4|57:4}}), but God promises victory ({{Psalm 91:13|91:13}}).
The psalmist does not claim to be without sin, but he knows that he does not deserve the cruel attacks of his opponents (see {{Psalm 35:7|35:7}}).
The psalmist declares his innocence, opening himself up to examination ({{Psalm 7:9|Psalm 7:9}}).

- *trample*: Compare {{Psalm 44:5|Psalm 44:5}}; {{Psalm 60:12|60:12}}; {{Psalm 91:13|91:13}}; {{Psalm 108:13|108:13}}. 

- *to the ground … in the dust*: Disgrace and shame can lead to death and the grave ({{Psalm 143:3|Psalm 143:3}}; see {{Psalm 13:3-4|13:3–4}}).
God’s judgment brings justice, despite the chaos created by enemies (see {{Psalm 7:11|7:11}}).
With this appeal to God for justice in the world, the psalmist also submits to God’s examination.

- The judgment is against the defendants (the peoples) and in favor of the righteous plaintiff (the psalmist; see {{Psalm 43:1|Psalm 43:1}}). 

- The psalmist, though not free from all sin, is a person of true integrity (see {{Psalm 15:2|Psalm 15:2}}; {{Psalm 25:21|25:21}}; {{Psalm 41:12|41:12}}; {{Psalm 78:72|78:72}}; compare {{Job 1:1|Job 1:1}}, {{Job 1:8|8}}; {{Job 9:20|9:20}}, {{Job 9:22|22}}).

God knows the thoughts and intentions of every person. He does not see only outward actions. He examines what is hidden in the mind and the heart (see {{Psalm 11:3-4|Psalms 11:3–4}}; {{Psalm 26:2|26:2}}; {{Psalm 139:1|139:1}}, {{Psalm 139:23|23}}).

The psalmist moves from his own situation ({{Psalm 7:1-9|Psalm 7:1–9}}) to speak for all the godly who seek redemption ({{Psalm 7:10-16|7:10–16}}). He protects and vindicates his people. When his followers cry out for help, God hears them and acts to rescue them.
The righteous judge cannot be bought or bribed. He does not abuse his power ({{Psalm 9:4|Psalm 9:4}}; compare {{Psalm 82:1-8|82:1–8}}).
*sword … bow … deadly weapons … arrows with fire*: As the Divine Warrior, God attacks to defend himself and his people.
Evil starts with small words or actions and leads to worse deeds over time (see {{Isaiah 59:4-5|Isaiah 59:4–5}}).

- *I will thank … sing praise*: The laments in {{Psalm 3:1-7:17|Psalms 3–7}} usually shift from lament to praise, as does the entire book of Psalms. 

- *Most High*: This is an ancient title for God (see {{Genesis 14:19|Genesis 14:19}}). 

- God is just and reliable, so his order prevails in this world.

- The LORD (Hebrew *Yahweh*) is the covenant God of Israel ({{Exodus 3:15|Exodus 3:15}}). This name emphasizes God’s faithfulness and relationship with his people.

He is also Lord (Hebrew *’adonay*), which emphasizes his authority. As Lord, he is the king over the earth and all creation. 

- The word translated as *majestic* (and sometimes *mighty*) can describe: 

- kings ({{Psalm 136:18|Psalm 136:18}}),

- heroes ({{Psalm 16:3|Psalm 16:3}}),

- mountains ({{Psalm 76:4|Psalm 76:4}}), or

- waves breaking on the seashore ({{Psalm 93:4|Psalm 93:4}}).

While all these things are awe-inspiring and mighty, they are less impressive than the Lord. 

- A person’s name represents their reputation. 

- The earth and the heavens reveal the Lord’s splendor. All creation worships and praises the Lord ({{Psalm 66:4|Psalm 66:4}}; {{Psalm 113:3|113:3}}; {{Psalm 145:21|145:21}}).

Psalm 8 praises God for being the creator of everything that exists. God created the heavens. This includes the heavenly world and spiritual beings like angels.

The heavens also include the sky with the moon and stars. Genesis 1 describes God making the lights in the sky. He made them to be rulers over the day and the night. They make sure that time and seasons work the way God wants them to.

Psalm 19 explains what happens when the sky does the work God gave it to do. The sun, moon and stars obey God’s commands about keeping day and night separate. That is how they tell everyone on earth about God’s glory. It’s how they show that the name of the Lord is majestic in the earth.

Having a majestic name means that God is great and wonderful. It means that God deserves honour everywhere on earth. It means that God has complete power and authority over everything. God chooses to share his authority with human beings.

Psalm 8 describes this as a crown that God placed on them. The crown is a sign that human beings are to be rulers. They are to be rulers over everything else that God created on earth. They are to make sure that what God wants done happens on earth. That is how they honour God and show that his name is majestic.

{{Psalm 8:1-9|Psalm 8}} begins the second part of Book One of the Psalms ({{Psalm 8:1-14:7|Psalms 8–14}}). The psalmist praises God’s creation and the dignity of the ideal human (see {{Psalm 1:1-6|Psalm 1}}). Instead of the world of enemies, wicked people, and unfair justice shown in {{Psalm 3:1-7:17|Psalms 3–7}}, this psalm presents the world as God first made it. Someone who is tired (both physically and emotionally) can imagine a place of dignity in God’s world.

- *silence*: The loud noise of the adversaries contrasts with the praise of God. In the end, the praise of God will overwhelm the sound of evil ({{Psalm 31:18|Psalms 31:18}}; {{Psalm 63:11|63:11}}; {{Psalm 101:5|101:5}}; {{Psalm 143:12|143:12}}). 

- Those who oppose God are filled with vengeful anger ({{Psalm 2:1-3|Psalm 2:1–3}}; {{Psalm 44:16|44:16}}; compare {{Psalm 149:6-7|149:6–7}}).

Many nations near Israel worshiped the sun, moon, and stars as gods. They thought these objects controlled life and events.

The psalmist reminds us that, while the sun, moon, and stars are great and beautiful, they are only created by God.

Because these things are his creation, they point to God’s power and majesty. They give a reason to praise the Almighty, who alone is worthy of worship.

God’s glory is vast and awe-inspiring. At first, it might seem that people are too small or unimportant to matter to him.

Yet God has given humans honor and dignity. He has crowned them with glory and set them in charge of creation. 

This shows that every person has value. Humans are called to care for and rule over the world responsibly, reflecting God’s glory in their lives.

*son of man *(literally *son of Adam*): This means "a human being." Through the influence of {{Daniel 7:13-14|Daniel 7:13–14}}, *son of man* became a title with divine meaning in the New Testament. See {{Hebrews 2:6-8|Hebrews 2:6–8}}, where this passage is quoted.

*You made him a little lower than the angels*: Humans bear God’s image. The Lord has given humans dignity and tasked them to rule ({{Genesis 1:26-27|Genesis 1:26–27}}). 

{{Hebrews 2:6-8|Hebrews 2:6–8}} applies these words to Jesus Christ, the ideal human who fully realized God’s purposes.

*made him ruler of the works of Your hands*: The psalmist is still referring to humans in general. 

Paul applies these words to Jesus as the perfect man who has made the created order, and even death ({{1 Corinthians 15:25-27|1 Corinthians 15:25–27}}), subject to God and his glory. 

The New Testament connects these themes of creation and salvation with Jesus Christ ({{John 1:1-2|John 1:1–2}}, {{John 1:14|14}}; {{Colossians 1:16|Colossians 1:16}}).

Wild animals, including birds and fish, remind us of God's creation of the animal world in {{Genesis 1:1-31|Genesis 1}}. Contrary to beliefs among Israel’s neighbors in the ancient Near East, animals are not sacred.

- The verb translated as *give thanks* is also translated as *thank* in {{Psalm 7:17|Psalm 7:17.}} This shows a strong connection between {{Psalm 7:1-17|Psalms 7}} and {{Psalm 9:1-20|9}} (see {{Psalm 7:17|7:17}}; {{Psalm 8:1-2|8:1–2}}). 

The phrase *with all my heart *shows the psalmist’s deep devotion and commitment ({{Psalm 86:12|Psalms 86:12}}; {{Psalm 111:1|111:1}}; {{Psalm 119:10|119:10}}; {{Psalm 138:1|138:1}}). 

- *I will recount*: These stories teach the next generation ({{Psalm 78:4|Psalms 78:4}}; {{Psalm 145:4|145:4}}). If forgotten, a generation might easily turn away from the Lord ({{Psalm 78:11|Psalms 78:11}}, {{Psalm 78:32|32}}). 

- *Your wonders*: These include the Lord’s judgments on the enemies of his people ({{Psalm 9:4|Psalm 9:4}}) and his care for the oppressed ({{Psalm 9:9|9:9}}). The wonders in creation, redemption, and revelation show his character and power ({{Psalm 89:5|Psalms 89:5}}; {{Psalm 111:4|111:4}}; {{Psalm 119:18|119:18}}, {{Psalm 119:27|27}}). His powerful acts inspire public praise ({{Psalm 9:1|Psalm 9:1}}; {{Psalm 26:7|26:7}}; {{Psalm 75:1|75:1}}).

However, that tune (or song) is no longer known. The same is true for the tunes mentioned in {{Psalm 22:1-31|Psalms 22}}, {{Psalm 45:1-17|45}}, {{Psalm 56:1-60:12|56–60}}, {{Psalm 69:1-36|69}}, {{Psalm 75:1-10|75}}, {{Psalm 80:1-19|and 80}}.

This hymn celebrates the Lord's rule and triumph over evil. It may also respond to the laments in {{Psalm 3:1-7:17|Psalms 3–7}}. 

Some believe that {{Psalm 9:1-20|Psalms 9}} and {{Psalm 10:1-18|10}} should be read together as one psalm in two parts. This is because {{Psalm 9:1-20|Psalm 9}} has a title, while {{Psalm 10:1-18|Psalm 10}} does not. 

Despite some missing or inverted letters, the two psalms form an acrostic of the Hebrew alphabet. This means that each line or section begins with a successive letter of the Hebrew alphabet.

Other alphabetic acrostics include {{Psalm 25:1-22|Psalms 25}}, {{Psalm 34:1-22|34}}, {{Psalm 37:1-40|37}}, {{Psalm 111:1-112:10|111–112}}, {{Psalm 119:1-176|119}}, and {{Psalm 145:1-21|145}}. 

The ancient Greek and Latin translations treat Psalms 9 and 10 as one psalm.

*rejoice … will sing praise*: The psalmist often connects joy with praises, as one leads to the other ({{Psalm 5:11-12|Psalm 5:11–12}}; {{Psalm 32:11|32:11}}; {{Psalm 67:4|67:4}}; {{Psalm 90:14|90:14}}; {{Psalm 92:4|92:4}}).
*retreat … stumble*: The Lord overpowers even powerful enemies (see {{Psalm 27:2|Psalm 27:2}}). Israel also experienced judgment when it resisted the Lord ({{Psalm 107:12|107:12}}).
The psalmist praises God's judgment of the wicked. This shows the Lord's promise to establish his kingdom on earth is trustworthy ({{Psalm 1:6|Psalms 1:6}}; {{Psalm 2:1-12|2}}).
The throne represents the Lord’s royal authority.

God created the heavens and the earth with a word ({{Genesis 1:1-31|Genesis 1}}), and he can end nations with a word (see {{Psalm 2:5|Psalm 2:5}}). 

Those who do evil will not endure forever. God promises that their power and influence will come to an end ({{Psalm 69:28|Psalm 69:28}}; {{Psalm 109:13|Psalm 109:13}}; {{Revelation 21:4|Revelation 21:4}}).

The godly do not rely on human governments, which can be weak or corrupt. They understand that earthly rulers are limited and sometimes unfair.

Instead, they put their hope in God’s eternal rule. God governs with perfect justice and fairness (see {{Psalm 96:1-100:5|Psalms 96–100}}).

- The Lord offers shelter in dangerous situations and protection from powerful and oppressive people. The psalms often describe the LORD as: 

- a fortress ({{Psalm 18:2|Psalm 18:2}}; {{Psalm 31:2|31:2}}),

- a rock ({{Psalm 18:2|Psalm 18:2}}; {{Psalm 42:9|42:9}}),

- strength ({{Psalm 18:1|Psalm 18:1}}), and

- a strong tower ({{Psalm 144:2|Psalm 144:2}}).

These images appear frequently in royal prayers (see {{Psalm 9:9|Psalm 9:9}}; {{Psalm 18:30|18:30}}).

- Even oppressed, afflicted, and marginalized people ({{Psalm 10:17|Psalm 10:17}}; {{Psalm 74:21|74:21}}) can receive divine protection. 

- Times of trouble ({{Psalm 10:1|Psalm 10:1}}; {{Psalm 20:1|20:1}}) contrast with moments when the Lord openly shows favor to the afflicted ({{Psalm 69:13|69:13}}; {{Psalm 102:13|102:13}}; see {{Psalm 107:6|Psalm 107:6}}).

At times, a person may feel separated from the Lord. The psalms describe moments of spiritual alienation or distress ({{Psalm 22:1|Psalms 22:1}}; {{Psalm 42:9|42:9}}; {{Psalm 119:8|119:8}})

Even in these times, the psalms affirm God’s faithfulness. The Lord does not abandon his people ({{Psalm 16:10|16:10}}; {{Psalm 37:25|37:25}}, {{Psalm 37:28|28}}).

The psalm writers often connect the idea that God dwells (or *sits,* or *is enthroned*) with a specific place, such as: 

- heaven ({{Psalm 2:4|Psalm 2:4}}; see {{Psalm 47:9|47:9}}),

- Jerusalem,

- "between the cherubim"({{Psalm 80:1|Psalms 80:1}}; {{Psalm 99:1|99:1}}),

- "on high" ({{Psalm 113:5|Psalm 113:5}}), or

- "at my right hand" ({{Psalm 110:1|Psalm 110:1}}).

Since the Lord rules the world, everyone must know about his unforgettable deeds of salvation (see {{Psalm 9:1|Psalm 9:1}}; {{Psalm 64:9|64:9}}; {{Psalm 66:16|66:16}}; {{Psalm 105:1|105:1}}).

Understanding that the Lord judges some wicked people ({{Psalm 9:3-6|Psalm 9:3–6}}) and promises to judge all evil ({{Psalm 9:7-10|9:7–10}}) inspires praise. The psalmist invites the godly community to join him.

The Lord saves his servants and punishes those who have harmed them ({{Psalm 18:46|Psalm 18:46}}). He defends his servants by fairly judging his enemies on earth ({{Psalm 58:11|Psalm 58:11}}). Those who follow God do not seek revenge. Instead, they wait for the Lord to defend them ({{Psalm 94:1-2|Psalm 94:1–2}}; {{Deuteronomy 32:35|Deuteronomy 32:35}}; {{Romans 12:19|Romans 12:19}}).

- The psalmist returns from a vision of the glorious future to the reality of facing his enemies ({{Psalm 9:3|Psalm 9:3}}). 

- The *gates* are a strong image of the powerful grip of death (see {{Psalm 13:3-4|Psalm 13:3–4}}). 

- The *gates of Daughter Zion* (that is, Jerusalem) provide an intentional contrast to the *gates of death*.

Hope requires waiting for the Lord’s rescue or justice ({{Psalm 25:3|Psalms 25:3}}, {{Psalm 25:5|5}}, {{Psalm 25:21|21}}). The godly experience hope, rest, and peace as they wait for the Lord (see {{Psalm 1:6|Psalm 1:6}}; {{Psalm 27:14|27:14}}).

- The psalmist concludes his lament by asking God to act on his behalf. He prays for the Lord’s intervention against those who do wrong. This includes a request for divine vengeance (God’s just punishment of evildoers). The psalmist trusts that only God can bring true justice.

- *but men*: People who gain power and honor can become oppressive and assume glory for themselves (see {{Psalm 8:4|Psalm 8:4}}; {{Psalm 10:18|10:18}}).

The opening questions set the mood. The Lord does not seem to hear the prayers of his people ({{Psalm 22:1|Psalm 22:1}}, {{Psalm 22:19|19}}; see {{2 Kings 4:27|2 Kings 4:27}}; {{Isaiah 1:15|Isaiah 1:15}}).

The lament in {{Psalm 9:13-20|Psalm 9:13–20}} continues in {{Psalm 10:1-18|Psalm 10}} (see study note on Psalms 9–10). However, the mood shifts from confident statements to anguished questions. The psalmist prays for rescue, trusting that the Lord, as a just king, take care of the needy.

The wicked openly defy God with their actions and words ({{Psalm 17:10|Psalm 17:10}}; {{Psalm 31:18|31:18}}; {{Psalm 59:12|59:12}}; {{Psalm 73:8|73:8}}; {{Psalm 123:4|123:4}}). Although the Lord will deal with them ({{Psalm 31:23|Psalm 31:23}}), they trouble the righteous (see {{Psalm 5:4-6|Psalm 5:4–6}}) before their condemnation and judgment.
Wicked and oppressive people might succeed, causing harmful effects. Evil can be as dramatic as the psalmist portrays it here, or it could be more subtle.
Unlike those who have evil desires, the godly wait for justice ({{Psalm 10:17|Psalm 10:17}}).
Even though they act wrongly ({{Psalm 5:9|Psalms 5:9}}; {{Psalm 28:3|28:3}}; {{Romans 3:14|Romans 3:14}}), the wicked still hope for a future free of trouble like the righteous will enjoy.
The wicked rely on violence ({{Psalm 11:5|Psalms 11:5}}; {{Psalm 37:32|37:32}}) and deception ({{Proverbs 12:6|Proverbs 12:6}}; {{Proverbs 23:27-28|23:27–28}}).
With confidence that the wicked will be held responsible for their deeds and that the Lord will care for the helpless, the psalmist prays intensely for rescue from evil.
The Lord cares for those who suffer. He will notice and punish those who do evil (see {{Psalm 72:14|Psalm 72:14}}; {{Psalm 116:15|116:15}}).

- The psalmist prays and calls for a strong curse (see “Prayers for Vengeance” Theme Note). 

- *Arms* represent the ability to wage war ({{Psalm 18:34|Psalms 18:34}}; {{Psalm 44:3|44:3}}).
As the true and just king, God will bring the wicked to an end, as he promises ({{Psalm 1:6|Psalm 1:6}}).
The psalmist expresses his confidence in the Lord.
People often misuse their power and enslave the very people God wants them to serve (see {{Psalm 9:19-20|Psalms 9:19–20}}; {{Luke 22:25-26|Luke 22:25–26}}).
